entities.summary:
William of Saint-Amour (c. 1202 – 1272-09-13) was a preeminent secular master of theology at the University of Paris and a central figure in the fierce mendicant controversy of the mid-13th century. His significance lies in his articulate, albeit ultimately condemned, opposition to the burgeoning power and privileges of the Dominican and Franciscan friars, challenging their right to teach, preach, and hear confessions within the traditional ecclesiastical structure. His arguments, rooted in a defense of the secular clergy's prerogatives and the established order, ignited a profound intellectual and institutional conflict that reverberated throughout medieval Christendom.

His most notable work, *De periculis novissimorum temporum* (On the Dangers of the Last Times), published around 1255, served as a scathing polemic against the mendicant orders. In it, William accused the friars of being false apostles, hypocrites, and even harbingers of the Antichrist, prophesied to appear in the 'last times.' He argued that their itinerant lifestyle, vows of poverty, and direct papal commissions undermined the authority of bishops and parish priests, usurping their pastoral duties and disrupting the hierarchical order of the Church. This treatise directly provoked the mendicant orders, especially Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, who penned vigorous rebuttals.
